findings.title: Options-object calls enable rejectOnClear by default despite documented default false
findings.cause: The options destructuring uses `rejectOnClear = true` when `concurrency` is an object, while the public Options docs/type declare `Default: false`.
findings.impact: Users who call `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` and later `clearQueue()` will unexpectedly reject every pending task with AbortError instead of only discarding the queue. Existing Promise.all users can see sudden rejections after upgrading even though they did not opt into rejection behavior.
findings.evidence: index.js:6-8 sets `rejectOnClear` to true for omitted options fields, and index.js:77-88 rejects queued promises when that flag is true. index.d.ts:99-106 and readme.md:46-51 document `rejectOnClear` as optional with default false.
findings.reproduction_or_test: No-install runtime probe using the current index.js with a stub Queue: create `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1})`, enqueue one never-settling task and one pending task, call `limit.clearQueue()`, then race the second promise against a timeout. Actual output was `clearQueueResult AbortError`; the documented default-false behavior would leave it pending.

findings.title: limit.map drops the mapper index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The map implementation gates the second mapper argument on `Array.isArray(iterable)`, passing `undefined` for Sets, iterator objects, and other supported iterables.
findings.impact: Any caller using the documented `limit.map(iterable, (item, index) => ...)` contract with a Set, generator, or iterator gets `undefined` indexes, causing wrong results, NaN arithmetic, bad keys, or cache collisions while TypeScript still promises `index: number`.
findings.evidence: index.js:107-112 computes `iterableIsArray` and passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`. The public contract in index.d.ts:30-42 and readme.md:78-84 says the mapper receives item value and index and is equivalent to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: No-install runtime probe using the current index.js with a stub Queue: `await pLimit(1).map(new Set(['a', 'b']), (value, index) => `${value}:${index}`)`. Actual output was `[ 'a:undefined', 'b:undefined' ]`; the documented equivalent Array.from mapping would produce `[ 'a:0', 'b:1' ]`.

findings.title: limitFunction returns a wrapper that discards all call arguments
findings.cause: The returned function is declared as `() => limit(() => function_())`, so it neither accepts nor forwards the arguments passed to the limited wrapper.
findings.impact: Reusable limited functions that depend on input parameters silently run with `undefined` arguments. This breaks the documented recipe `urls.map(url => limitedFetchUrl(url))` and contradicts the generic TypeScript signature, making production fetchers, API calls, and keyed work items fail or operate on undefined input.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-124 drops wrapper arguments. index.d.ts:133-136 returns `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`, index.test-d.ts:25-26 type-checks calling the wrapper with an argument, and recipes.md:151-163 demonstrates `limitedFetchUrl(url)` forwarding a URL to the original function.
findings.reproduction_or_test: No-install runtime probe using the current index.js with a stub Queue: `const limited = limitFunction(async (value, suffix) => `${value}:${suffix}`, {concurrency: 1}); await limited('x', 'y')`. Actual output was `undefined:undefined`; expected output is `x:y`.
